title: Natan Sharansky
hookLine: a refusenik imprisoned for years, then freed

cards: The last order the guards give him is simple: walk straight across the bridge, to the car on the other side. It's a cold morning on the edge of Berlin, and he stands at one end.
He has spent years in Soviet prisons doing what he was told, or refusing to. He sets off across the bridge, and he walks in a zigzag. A tiny act.
By his own account, it was on purpose. His name is Natan Sharansky.

teach.b: He was called Anatoly then, a young mathematician in Moscow who loved chess. He applied to emigrate to Israel and was refused.

He became a refusenik, and then a voice for others, meeting foreign reporters and speaking up for human rights. He was arrested and accused of spying, a charge he denied and his supporters called false.
He spent years in prisons and labor camps, including long stretches in punishment cells, cold and alone.
Meanwhile his wife, Avital, already in Israel, traveled from country to country saying his name to anyone who would listen. What kept him going inside?
He has written that the guards could control his body but not his inner world. He played chess games in his head.
And he had a small book of Psalms that reached him from Avital.
When guards took it away, he fought to get it back. Years later he called his memoir by a line from that book: Fear No Evil.
It comes from Psalm 23: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, For Thou art with me." A cell can hold a body.
In his telling, it never held his choices: what to think about, what to refuse, what to keep. The zigzag on the bridge was one more of them, made in plain sight of the guards.

how: Psalm 23 is said by Jews at the third Sabbath meal and in times of fear and mourning, and Sharansky's story is retold as part of the history of the movement for Soviet Jewry.

games.q: you are being released across a bridge in Berlin after years in prison. the guards tell you: walk straight to the car. what do you do?
games.why: by his own account, Sharansky zigzagged across: one last small choice the guards didn't make for him.

practice: Bring to mind one place in your life that feels like a small cell: a job you can't leave yet, an illness, a family tangle, a long wait.

Don't fight it for now; just find one thing inside it that is still yours, your breath, your kindness, a line you choose to remember, the way you answer, and hold it. If you pray, you can say the psalm's words: I will fear no evil.

wordCard.voice: Natan Sharansky. A refusenik imprisoned for years in the Soviet Union, who held on to his book of Psalms and walked to freedom in a zigzag.

orig.note: Hebrew: I will fear no evil, from Psalm 23.

carryVoice: Your line: free inside. Even a walk across a bridge can be a choice. Until tomorrow.
